examples.solution_text:
(a) The vertices are $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$, so there are $4$ vertices.
There are three edges $AB$, then $BC$, $CD$, $DA$, $AC$ and the loop at $B$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}3+1+1+1+1+1\\&=8\end{aligned}$ edges.
(b) At $A$, the three edges to $B$ and the edges to $C$ and $D$ give $d(A)=5$.
At $B$, the three edges to $A$, the edge to $C$ and both ends of the loop give $d(B)=6$.
At $C$, the edges to $A$, $B$ and $D$ give $d(C)=3$.
At $D$, the edges to $A$ and $C$ give $d(D)=2$.
(c) $\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}5+6+3+2\\&=16\end{aligned}$.
(d) No. There is no edge joining $B$ and $D$.
(e) The vertices represent towns.
The edges represent roads connecting the towns, including the loop road.

Drawing 1 joins $JK$, $JN$, $KL$, $KN$, $LN$ and $LM$.
Drawing 2 joins the same six pairs.
Yes. The vertices have moved, but every connection is unchanged.

(a) The degree represents the number of direct flight routes available from that airport.
(b) The edges at $P$ lead to $Q$, $R$, $S$, $T$ and $U$.
There are $5$ direct flight routes from $P$.
(c) $d(P)=5$.
$d(Q)=2$, from $QP$ and $QR$.
$d(R)=2$, from $RP$ and $RQ$.
$d(S)=1$, from $SP$.
$d(T)=2$, from $TP$ and $TU$.
$d(U)=2$, from $UP$ and $UT$.
Airport $P$ has the most direct flight routes because it has the highest degree.
(d) $P$ and $S$ have odd degrees, $5$ and $1$.
There are $2$ vertices of odd degree.
$Q$, $R$, $T$ and $U$ each have degree $2$.
There are $4$ vertices of even degree.

(a) Only the marked dots are vertices. The unmarked crossing adds no vertex and does not split either road.
There are $5$ vertices. The edges are $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$, $AC$, $BD$ and $CE$, so there are $7$ edges.
(b) $d(A)=3$, $d(B)=3$, $d(C)=4$, $d(D)=3$ and $d(E)=1$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}3+3+4+3+1\\&=14\end{aligned}$.
Each edge contributes two ends to the degree sum. The check gives $2\times7=14$, which agrees.
